cover.label: SAME PRICE SINCE THE 1980s
cover.headline: Costco refuses to raise this price. It's {the smartest move in retail.}

slides.label: THE DEAL
slides.headline: A hot dog and a soda. {$1.50.} Since the 1980s.
slides.body: The price never moved, while inflation kept going. In today's dollars, that 1980s $1.50 would be *roughly $4.50.* So why does Costco hold the line?

slides.label: THE TWIST
slides.quote: If you raise the effing hot dog, I will kill you. {Figure it out.}
slides.by: — JIM SINEGAL, CO-FOUNDER (AS TOLD BY CRAIG JELINEK)
slides.body: Jelinek reportedly wanted to raise the price because Costco was losing money on it.
slides.source: Craig Jelinek interview, 2018, as reported by Fortune / NPR

slides.label: THE SECRET
slides.headline: The real profit is {in the membership card.}
slides.body: In fiscal 2025, Costco collected *$5.3 billion* in membership fees. That's *about half* of its $10.4 billion operating income. The hot dog gets you in. ==The card pays the bills.==

slides.label: HOW THEY DO IT
rows: *Costco swaps Hebrew National* for its own Kirkland Signature franks to keep costs down.
Food courts have *swapped soda suppliers* to keep drink costs low. The price stays.
Costco's CFO says the $1.50 price is *“safe.”*
slides.source: Fortune; Food Republic; Costco earnings call (June 2024)

last.headline: One cheap product can {sell the whole store.}
last.body: A loss leader isn't a loss if it keeps members paying every year.
